content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

This is a fresh first cycle — no prior artifacts. I'm acting as your **Facilitator** and we're at the very first step: understanding what you really want before anything gets built.

Let me start with the goal itself, not the features.

You said you want to save and manage bookmarks. Before I picture *how* it works, I'd like to understand *why* you want it and what should feel different once it exists.

A few things I'm wondering:

- **Today**, how do you keep track of links you want to come back to — and what goes wrong with that? (For example: they pile up in your browser, you can never find the one you need, they're scattered across devices, etc.)
- **When this app is finished and working well**, what's the moment where you'd think "yes, this is exactly what I needed"? What are you doing in that moment?
- Is **"saving and managing bookmarks"** truly the heart of it — or is that the means to something bigger, like actually *rediscovering and reading* the things you saved, or *sharing* collections with others?

You don't need to answer in any structured way — just tell me in your own words what's on your mind. That'll set our direction, and from there I'll show you a working screen you can actually click through rather than making you read specifications.

Right now my browser bookmarks are a cluttered pile, and links also end up scattered across notes and open tabs. I often remember what a page was about but not its exact title, so finding it again is frustrating.

The “yes, this is exactly what I needed” moment would be saving a link quickly, having the useful details filled in for me, and then finding it months later by searching a few remembered words or choosing a tag. I’d also like to separate things I intend to read from things I’m keeping as a reference, and tidy old links away without necessarily deleting them.

So the heart of it is personal saving and rediscovery, rather than sharing with other people. I’d like it to feel like a calm, searchable library of links, not another overflowing bookmark folder.

That's a clear and vivid picture — thank you. Let me play back what I understood, in plain terms, so we're aligned on direction:

**The goal:** a calm, personal library of links — where the pain of the cluttered browser pile is replaced by *trusting* that anything you save can be found again later.

The things that would make it feel right:

1. **Saving is quick**, and the app fills in the useful details for you rather than making you type them.
2. **Rediscovery works from fuzzy memory** — you find a link months later by searching a few words you half-remember, or by picking a tag, even if you've forgotten the exact title.
3. **Two kinds of links live differently** — things you *intend to read* versus things you're *keeping as reference* — kept separate rather than mixed in one pile.
4. **Tidying away ≠ deleting** — you can retire old links out of sight without losing them.
5. It's **personal** — for you rediscovering your own things, not sharing with others.

Is that the right direction? If any of it is off, or you'd phrase the heart of it differently, tell me now — everything we build rests on this.

And one thing I need to picture it concretely: **where do you imagine using this?** For example, in a web browser on your computer, as a phone app, as something on your desktop, or something else? You mentioned your browser and open tabs, so a browser-based version comes to mind — but I don't want to assume.

Yes, that’s the right direction. By “things I intend to read,” I mean a link can be marked unread and shown in its own view; once I’ve read it, it should leave that view but remain in my library.

## We've reached a natural point to build. Here's the full settled scope — in plain terms:

**Saving & keeping links accurate**
1. Paste a link (shorthand like `nytimes.com` is fine); review auto-filled title, description, preview image, icon, and date before saving.
2. Bad addresses are refused; you're never left with a broken item.
3. Saving a link you already have takes you to the existing one instead of duplicating.
4. Edit a link's title, description, and personal note anytime.
5. Change a link's address later, review the new page, and keep your own wording unless you adopt the fetched version.

**Reading vs. reference**
6. Flag links "To read"; reading one moves it to Reference; everything lives in one library.

**Rediscovery**
7. Tags with reuse suggestions and include/exclude filtering.
8. A dependable search (phrases, `#tag`, `and/or/not`, parentheses) across title, description, address, and note.
9. A personal **Markdown note**, separate from the page's description.

**Managing a larger library**
10. Archive to tidy away (never lose); delete only from the archive, confirmed.
11. Sort (newest, recently updated, oldest, title).
12. Bulk actions on many links, including "select all matching."
13. Saved views from search + include/exclude tags, kept live.
14. Import/export standard browser bookmarks (with folders → tags).
15. Display preferences (default order, links per page, text size), synced to your library.

**Two honest boundaries I'll hold to:**
- **Preserved page copies & Internet Archive** — the *experience* is approved, but the real page-storage and archive.org connection are a **separate follow-up cycle**; this build won't fake them.
- Because your library and preferences **sync across devices**, the build rests on an **account-based, synced store** — I'll treat that as foundational.

That's **15 settled feature flows**. **May I switch from exploring to actually building this scope?** I won't start until you say so.

- Refuse malformed addresses, but if a valid page cannot be reached, let me enter its details manually and save it.

- Cross-device sync is for my single personal library and preferences. I don’t need sharing, multiple-user administration, or self-service account management in this cycle.

## ✅ Your Link Library is ready to review

**Open it here: http://maker:4000**

It starts as a calm, empty library — paste a link to begin. It's a real working app now (not the exploratory prototype): your links, tags, notes, saved views, and preferences live on the server, so the same library appears on any device you open it from.

### What was built — the 15 behaviours you approved
- **Saving:** paste a link (shorthand like `nytimes.com` works); it fetches the real page's title, description, preview image, icon, and date for you to review and adjust before saving. If a page can't be reached, you fill the details in by hand rather than being blocked. Bad addresses are refused; duplicates take you to the existing entry.
- **Editing:** change title, description, note, tags, reading state, or the address later — an address change re-fetches for review while keeping your own wording.
- **Reading vs. reference**, the temporary "To read" flag, and one unified library.
- **Rediscovery:** tag reuse suggestions, include/exclude tag filters, and the full search language (phrases, `#tag`, case-insensitive `and/or/not`, parentheses), plus a **Markdown note** separate from the page description.
- **Managing at scale:** archive/restore (delete only from the archive, confirmed), sorting, bulk actions with "select all matching," saved views, browser-bookmark import/export (folders → tags), and display preferences (default order, links per page, text size) synced to your library.

### Verification outcome (plain language)
- **Internal quality tests: 19/19 passed** (address rules, search grammar, Markdown safety, bookmark import/export, storage & sync).
- **Behaviour acceptance tests: 23/23 passed**, covering every approved scenario, with **no runtime errors**.
- **Sync confirmed:** the library and preferences persist server-side and are served identically to any device.

### Held to our agreed boundaries
- **Preserved page copies & Internet Archive** are **not** in this build — recorded as a dedicated follow-up cycle (LATER-002). No buttons pretend to preserve.
- Single personal library with cross-device sync; no sharing, multi-user admin, or self-service account management this cycle.
